items.stem: Explain why a date of birth should be stored as DATE rather than as text.
items.answer: A DATE field validates that the value is a real date, sorts chronologically rather than alphabetically, and allows date arithmetic such as calculating age; text such as "03/04/2008" is ambiguous and sorts incorrectly.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A DATE field validates that the value is a real date, sorts chronologically rather than alphabetically, and allows date arithmetic such as calculating age; text such as "03/04/2008" is ambiguous and sorts incorrectly. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

items.answer: 55 bytes per record; 440000 bytes ≈ 429.7 KiB

items.stem: A charity in Mumbai keeps volunteer details in a spreadsheet with columns VolunteerName, Phone, Event1, Event1Date, Event2, Event2Date. Describe three problems with this design and explain how a relational design would solve them.
items.answer: Problems: repeating groups (Event1, Event2…) limit the number of events and waste space; event details are duplicated for every volunteer (redundancy) so changing an event date needs many edits (update anomaly) and can cause inconsistency; no unique identifier, so two volunteers with the same name cannot be told apart. Relational design: Volunteer(VolunteerID PK, Name, Phone), Event(EventID PK, Name, Date), Attendance(VolunteerID FK, EventID FK) with composite PK – each fact stored once and any number of events per volunteer.
items.markingKey: Problems: repeating groups (Event1, Event2…) limit the number of events and waste space; event details are duplicated for every volunteer (redundancy) so changing an event date needs many edits (update anomaly) and can cause inconsistency; no unique identifier, so two volunteers with the same name cannot be told apart. Relational design: Volunteer(VolunteerID PK, Name, Phone), Event(EventID PK, Name, Date), Attendance(VolunteerID FK, EventID FK) with composite PK – each fact stored once and any number of events per volunteer.

items.stem:
Case study context: MetroFlow, the public-transport authority in Kuala Lumpur, stores ticketing data in a data warehouse, predicts passenger demand with machine learning and runs route-planning software built from classes and graph structures.
(a) Distinguish between CHAR(n) and VARCHAR(n). Refer to MetroFlow in your answer. [2]
(b) To what extent is it true that a spreadsheet is an adequate replacement for a relational database in a small business? Refer to MetroFlow in your answer. [4]
items.answer: (a) CHAR(n) always reserves n characters (padding shorter values); VARCHAR(n) stores only the characters entered, up to n, so it saves space for values of varying length. (b) Adequate only for very small, single-user data; once data are related and shared, a relational DBMS is needed for integrity, security and concurrency.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] CHAR(n) always reserves n characters (padding shorter values); VARCHAR(n) stores only the characters entered, up to n, so it saves space for values of varying length. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions). (b) [4 marks] Arguments for: easy to set up and familiar to staff; adequate for a small amount of data used by one person. Arguments against: no enforced relationships or referential integrity; redundant data leads to inconsistencies; weak multi-user access control and concurrency; does not scale and lacks a query language such as SQL. Supported judgement: Adequate only for very small, single-user data; once data are related and shared, a relational DBMS is needed for integrity, security and concurrency. items.stem: A hospital in Lisbon stores Doctor(DoctorID, Name, Specialism), Patient(PatientID, Name, DOB) and Appointment(…). Each appointment is for one patient with one doctor at a date and time. Design the Appointment table, identifying its primary key and foreign keys, and justify your choices.
items.answer: Appointment(AppointmentID PK, PatientID FK → Patient, DoctorID FK → Doctor, AppDate, AppTime, Room). AppointmentID is a surrogate key because a patient may see the same doctor many times (so PatientID+DoctorID is not unique); alternatively a composite key (DoctorID, AppDate, AppTime) is a candidate key since a doctor cannot have two appointments at once. PatientID and DoctorID are foreign keys giving two 1:M relationships and enforcing referential integrity.

items.stem: Explain how record locking prevents the lost update problem.
items.answer: The first transaction to update a record obtains a lock; the second must wait until the first commits and releases it, then reads the updated value, so both changes are applied in sequence.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Optimistic concurrency control (checking for conflicts only at commit) is better than pessimistic locking for an online shop."
items.answer: Optimistic control suits read-heavy workloads with rare conflicts; pessimistic locking is safer for high-contention records such as stock levels of popular items.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: most transactions do not conflict, so no time is wasted waiting for locks; better throughput and no deadlocks. Arguments against: when conflicts are frequent (e.g. last items in stock) many transactions must be restarted; users may lose work if their transaction is rejected at commit. Supported judgement: Optimistic control suits read-heavy workloads with rare conflicts; pessimistic locking is safer for high-contention records such as stock levels of popular items.

items.stem: The sample links between Doctor and Patient records are: D2–p4, D1–p2, D1–p1, D3–p3, D2–p1. Assuming the sample is typical, identify the type of relationship between Doctor and Patient and describe how it should be implemented in a relational database.
items.answer: M:N (Doctor to Patient); implement with a junction table DoctorPatient(DoctorID, PatientID) with a composite primary key, each part a foreign key.
items.markingKey: M:N (Doctor to Patient); implement with a junction table DoctorPatient(DoctorID, PatientID) with a composite primary key, each part a foreign key. 1 mark for the relationship type with reasoning from the data (an Doctor appears more than once, a Patient appears more than once); 1-2 marks for the implementation.

items.stem:
A Patient table is being designed. For each field below, state the most appropriate data type and justify your choice.
IsMember: e.g. TRUE, FALSE, TRUE
Email: e.g. li.wei@mail.sg, k.mensah@uni.gh, a.ruiz@correo.pe
LastLogin: e.g. 2026-05-02 08:15:00, 2026-05-03 19:42:10, 2026-05-04 06:01:55
items.answer: IsMember – BOOLEAN because it only ever has two possible values; Email – VARCHAR(100) because it is text of varying length; LastLogin – DATETIME / TIMESTAMP because it records both a date and a time

items.stem:
(a) Define the term "concurrency control". [2]
(b) Explain the difference between referential integrity and entity integrity. [2]
(c) For each event, identify the type of integrity rule that is broken and explain why.
1. two Product records are given ProductID P17
2. a Department row is deleted while Staff rows still reference it
3. an Order is inserted with CustomerID 908, but no customer 908 exists [3]
items.answer: (a) DBMS mechanisms, such as locking or timestamps, that let several users work on the same data at the same time without corrupting it (b) Entity integrity requires a unique, non-NULL primary key in every table; referential integrity requires every foreign key to match an existing primary key in the referenced table. (c) 1. entity integrity – primary key values must be unique; 2. referential integrity – deleting a referenced parent leaves orphan child records; 3. referential integrity – a foreign key must match an existing primary key

items.stem: A national pension fund in Oslo records contributions and payouts for every citizen. Recommend a database model for this organisation, justifying your choice.
items.answer: Recommended: relational. Reasons: highly structured, related financial data needing ACID transactions, referential integrity and auditable SQL reporting; eventual consistency would be unacceptable for money; volume is large but manageable for a relational DBMS.
items.markingKey: Recommended: relational. items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that Natural keys should always be preferred to surrogate keys.
items.answer: Not always: surrogate keys are usually safer as primary keys, while natural candidate keys can still be protected with UNIQUE constraints.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: natural keys carry meaning and avoid an extra column; they prevent duplicate entry of the same real-world item. Arguments against: natural values can change, forcing cascading updates; they may be long text, slowing joins and indexes; uniqueness is not always guaranteed (e.g. names, emails reused). Supported judgement: Not always: surrogate keys are usually safer as primary keys, while natural candidate keys can still be protected with UNIQUE constraints.

items.stem: "A spreadsheet is an adequate replacement for a relational database in a small business." Discuss.
items.answer: Adequate only for very small, single-user data; once data are related and shared, a relational DBMS is needed for integrity, security and concurrency.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: easy to set up and familiar to staff; adequate for a small amount of data used by one person. Arguments against: no enforced relationships or referential integrity; redundant data leads to inconsistencies; weak multi-user access control and concurrency; does not scale and lacks a query language such as SQL. Supported judgement: Adequate only for very small, single-user data; once data are related and shared, a relational DBMS is needed for integrity, security and concurrency. items.stem:
Case study context: MetroFlow, the public-transport authority in Kuala Lumpur, stores ticketing data in a data warehouse, predicts passenger demand with machine learning and runs route-planning software built from classes and graph structures.
(a) Explain the difference between verification and validation. Refer to MetroFlow in your answer. [2]
(b) To what extent is it true that Optimistic concurrency control (checking for conflicts only at commit) is better than pessimistic locking for an online shop? Refer to MetroFlow in your answer. [4]
items.answer: (a) Validation checks that data is reasonable and obeys rules (range, type, format) when entered; verification checks that data has been copied or entered accurately, e.g. double entry or proof-reading against the source. (b) Optimistic control suits read-heavy workloads with rare conflicts; pessimistic locking is safer for high-contention records such as stock levels of popular items.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Validation checks that data is reasonable and obeys rules (range, type, format) when entered; verification checks that data has been copied or entered accurately, e.g. double entry or proof-reading against the source. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions). (b) [4 marks] Arguments for: most transactions do not conflict, so no time is wasted waiting for locks; better throughput and no deadlocks. Arguments against: when conflicts are frequent (e.g. last items in stock) many transactions must be restarted; users may lose work if their transaction is rejected at commit. Supported judgement: Optimistic control suits read-heavy workloads with rare conflicts; pessimistic locking is safer for high-contention records such as stock levels of popular items. items.stem:
Case study context: Aurora Energy, a utility in Toronto, collects smart-meter readings in a distributed database, detects faults with anomaly detection and models its devices as objects in a simulation.
(a) Explain the difference between a document database and a relational database. Refer to Aurora Energy in your answer. [2]
(b) "Eventual consistency is acceptable for every web application." To what extent do you agree with this statement? Refer to Aurora Energy in your answer. [4]
items.answer: (a) A relational database stores data in fixed-schema tables linked by keys and queried with SQL joins; a document database stores self-contained, flexible JSON-like documents that can nest related data, avoiding joins. (b) Acceptable only where short-lived stale data has low cost; not for transactions involving money or limited resources.

(b) [4 marks] Arguments for: improves availability and speed; users rarely notice short delays in, e.g., like counts. Arguments against: financial balances, stock and bookings must be consistent immediately; stale reads can cause double bookings or overspending. Supported judgement: Acceptable only where short-lived stale data has low cost; not for transactions involving money or limited resources.
